That's the nature of the job. It's solving problems that have not been solved yet. If you encounter a problem you've already solved, you abstract it away in a function or a class and then use those as your building blocks. And so on.

No wonder programmers are stressed -- no other job is like this and the boss demands you estimate how long this thing you've never done before will take or just gives you a deadline.

Another thing is that humans are really bad at estimating things that will take them longer than maybe 4 hours. The only way for us to effectively train our brain to estimate something is to have relatively immediate feedback on whether we were successful in our estimate or not. The minute something takes you longer than a day, that estimate is gone as far as your brain is concerned. There's no neural pruning that's going to happen when you finally finish it, because you likely don't care what that original estimate was, you just care that now the task/project is finished.

Side note: This is the logic behind the silicon valley craze of "agile" programming, which on the surface is sound; although as far as I've seen it ends up creating an even more stressful work environment for already incredibly stressed people.

Many of the jobs posted in my area are asking for someone with experience. What kinds of businesses should I be looking for?
Places to find entry level receptionist jobs?
Make a linked-in, you can narrow your searches by experience level

Absolutely apply for whatever is available. If you have answered a phone, you have experience. Make sure you have basic computer skills (word, excel) and dress for business when interviewed. Remember that you will be the face of the company when people call and visit so dress nice and speak clearly. Questions to ask are daily volume of calls and position exceptions. Reception can be a stressful position if it's a busy company but in the end you just deal with one call at a time and go from there. I've seen many receptionists close to tears from the stress. My favorite trick is to unplug the main switchboard which resets the system. It gives the receptionist a couple of minutes to breath while it restarts and reinforces concept that it's not the end of the world of someone gets cut off.
Good luck!
